blocks.text: She labors in vain, without fear] Mothers are said to have labored in vain when they bear children who will not live. So Esa. LXV, 23. They shall not labor in vain, nor bring forth for trouble. So in the Agamemnon of Aeschylus the vultures grieve over their stolen young, δεμνιοτήρη πόνον ὀρταλίχων ὀλέσαντες [demniotērē ponon ortalichōn olesantes], having lost the labor they had spent in guarding the nest of their chicks. In this same sense Job writes that the ostrich labors in vain when it neglects the eggs it has laid, not without labor: namely, because it is without fear. Not without all fear, for the ostrich is a most timid animal. Accordingly, among the Arabs one of the various names of the ostrich is اجفيل [ijfīl] igphil, as if you were to say timid. Alcamus: الاجفيل الجبن والظليم ينفر من كل شي [al-ijfīl al-jabān wa-al-ẓalīm yanfiru min kull shī], Igphil, that is, timid; also the male ostrich, which flees for any cause whatever. There is also an Arabic proverb, اجبن [II, 861] نعامة من اجبن [ajban naʿāma min ajban], more timid than an ostrich: خافت انها لانها وذلك ابدا اليه ترجع لا موضع من [khāfat annahā li-annahā wa-dhālika abadan ilayhi tarjiʿ lā mawḍiʿ min], and this because, when it flees from some place out of fear, it never returns there. So Damir in the section On Proverbs. But here the ostrich is said to be devoid of fear, because it lacks that provident fear by which parents are driven to look out for their young. This fear springs from love. Ovid in the Epistle of Penelope:
Love is a thing full of anxious fear.
And this fear always keeps parents anxious and troubled. Hence that father in the Comic poet:
I, because my son has not come back, what things I think of, and by what things I am now troubled: lest he has caught cold, or fallen somewhere, or broken something.

But the ostrich, because it does not love, likewise does not fear for its young. As soon as it has left the nest, it forgets its own eggs and sits on those of others with the same affection as on its own. But, you will say, in Aelian (Hist. book 14, ch. 7) the ostrich is described as ἐρῶσα τῶν νεοττῶν ἰσχυρῶς, καὶ διψῶσα αὐτῶν τῆς συνουσίας [erōsa tōn neottōn ischyrōs, kai dipsōsa autōn tēs synousias], loving its chicks intensely, and thirsting for their company, that is, supremely eager for it. So much so that, returning from foraging, although it finds the nest fenced about by the hunter with iron points, nevertheless νικωμένη ὑπὸ τοῦ ἱμέρου, καὶ οἰστρουμένη [nikōmenē hypo tou himerou, kai oistroumenē], overcome by longing for them, and roused as if by a gadfly, it rushes with spread wings, running and screeching, into the midst of the iron, and so, pierced by its own onrush, perishes miserably. I reply that, of all the writers who have treated the ostrich, Aelian alone reports this; and that he could have been deceived in this report just as in what precedes it, that the ostrich lays ὑπὲρ τὰ ὀγδοή- [col. 256] κοντα [hyper ta ogdoēkonta], more than eighty eggs, whereas Alkazuinius reckons only twenty, and Leo Africanus and Marmolius only ten or twelve. Or, if the story is true, that it is the effect not of love but of stupidity that the ostrich rushes onto the iron with so blind an impulse. Of this stupidity there follows in Job:
